title: Bryan Caplan Is Wrong About Pedagogy
author: Jack Despain Zhou
summary: In this Theories of Progress essay, Jack Despain Zhou grants that Bryan Caplan is strongest on the economics of signaling in The Case Against Education, but argues that the book's picture of how students learn is superficial and incurious. He traces the disagreement to their childhoods, since Caplan decided school was pointless while Zhou loved learning and wanted school to work, so one concluded we need less school and the other better school. He says Caplan inverts K. Anders Ericsson, whose research found little improvement from experience alone and called for purpose-built training institutions. On online learning, he argues that the internet enables whims and rarely gives the structure needed for the strenuous middle stage of talent development, drawing on his own experience with Chinese, law school and online charters, and on data from virtual schools and COVID. He rejects Caplan's view that pedagogy is both unimportant and already solved, pointing to Direct Instruction, Art of Problem Solving and Mississippi's phonics reforms as concrete improvements. He closes by endorsing a rebuilt approach to schools of education.
points: Caplan's case against education treats pedagogy as inconsequential and solved, yet the cases for or against schooling depend on how people actually learn.
Ericsson's research on deliberate practice shows that time on the job rarely improves performance without coaching and structured practice, which supports purpose-built institutions.
The internet suits exploration and whims but seldom gives the structure and accountability that the long, strenuous stage of skill development needs.
Online charters and pandemic remote learning produced large losses, so removing social structure tends to hurt students, especially younger and less experienced ones.
Direct Instruction, Art of Problem Solving and Mississippi's phonics reforms show that targeted changes to teaching can improve outcomes even inside resistant systems.
quotes: When he does venture into pedagogy, he presents a superficial and incurious picture of how students actually learn.
He concluded we need less school; I concluded we need better school.
This is an inversion of Ericsson’s work — replicating, in fact, the very misconception that inspired much of Ericsson’s research in the first place.
In many professional domains, people do not meaningfully improve given more time on the job.
The internet is a wonderful enabler of our short-term whims, and a mediocre pedagogue that very rarely provides the structure an optimal education demands.

Self-structured online learning rewards play and exploration and empowers original research, but in the strenuous stage needed for real talent acquisition, people benefit immensely from deliberate structure and real accountability.
You can’t even get the public to back firing teachers, and you want to tear the whole education system down?

Pedagogy is neither so well-understood nor so hopeless as Caplan would say. Education has never been a mature science, and outsiders working from first principles often make jumps that would be unthinkable in more developed domains.
